overview: This atlas label groups parts of the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra and Java between 600 and 800. “Under Indian influence” describes cultural connections, not rule by an Indian government or a single local state. The polygons include tested points at Kedah, Palembang, Kota Kapur and Dieng, while clipping other important places such as Borobudur and Batujaya. Ports, rulers and religious communities used ideas and scripts from South Asia in their own settings. Srivijaya, early Javanese courts and Kedah remain distinct histories; the later regional umbrella beginning in 800 has a different outline and its own card.

periods.title: Ports and inscriptions
periods.summary: Kedukan Bukit records a ruler’s expedition in 682, within a region of distinct political centers.

periods.title: Building and continuing connections
periods.summary: Dieng’s early temple phases extended through much of the eighth century.

items.text: The Chinese monk Yijing sailed from Guangzhou in 671 on a Persian ship and visited Srivijaya before continuing toward India. His route included Kacha, usually identified with Kedah, where he used a merchant vessel. Religious travel depended on commercial shipping: a pilgrimage could require negotiating the same winds and ports as a cargo voyage.

The Kedukan Bukit stone near Palembang records a 682 expedition associated with Dapunta Hyang. Its account combines river travel, people walking, supplies and the making of a wanua, or settlement. The precise route and some readings remain debated. It shows organized movement and political ambition, rather than proving that the entire atlas polygon belonged to Srivijaya.

A 686 inscription at Kota Kapur on Bangka threatens those who betray Srivijaya’s ruler or his appointed authorities. It mentions a military expedition against Bhumi Jawa. The wording records an intention and an assertion of power; it is not a complete campaign diary establishing the conquest of every part of Java.

The Kota Kapur text is arranged in ten lines on a tall stone. To read its lines from left to right in their normal orientation, a reader would lay the stone with its pointed end to the left. Inscriptions need careful looking as well as language knowledge: even deciding which way is up can matter.

sections.title: A garden, households and practical craft

items.text: The Talang Tuwo inscription, dated 684, describes a garden established by Sri Jayanasa near Palembang. Its plants included coconut, areca, sugar palm, sago and bamboo, with other gardens, dams and ponds also mentioned. The text wishes that travelers find food and drinking water. This is a royal dedication and statement of intent, not a measured report of every person’s diet.

That dedication also wishes for thriving fields, livestock, trustworthy friends and faithful spouses, and freedom from illness and disturbed sleep. Its hopes reveal everyday anxieties alongside Buddhist aspirations. Enslaved people appear among possessions expected to prosper, exposing the unequal society behind royal benevolence. Wishes for health do not establish a hospital or prove that disease had been prevented.

At Sungai Mas in Kedah, researchers compared the material in ancient bricks with clay from the Muda River basin. The similarities support local manufacture. Temple building drew on regional skills and raw materials, even while religious ideas traveled widely. An imported idea did not require importing every brick needed to put it into practice.

A large granite jar found beside the sanctuary steps at Sungai Mas has been interpreted as a water container for visitors to wash their feet. It belonged to a complex with additions over several centuries; the associated makara is dated broadly to the seventh through ninth centuries. This is a site-specific interpretation of ritual cleanliness, not evidence for toilets in every home.

Glass lumps and finished beads at Sungai Mas point to manufacture as well as trade. Compositional studies compare the glass with material from other regions rather than declaring every bead an import. Producing these small ornaments required control of materials and technique. Their size can hide the amount of skilled work involved.

sections.title: Temples, water and a written word

items.text: Dieng’s temples stand on a volcanic plateau about 2,000 meters above sea level. Heritage researchers place early construction in the late seventh and early eighth centuries, with further work continuing later in the eighth. Sacred buildings here belonged to a Javanese setting far from the coastal ports. The plural map label should not flatten these different landscapes into one capital.

Ancient channels are part of Dieng’s archaeological landscape. Much later, nineteenth-century investigators encountered temples standing in water, and recovery involved drainage and excavation. These traces make water management part of the site’s story, but they do not prove that all channels were built at the same time or carried household sewage.

A small Old Malay word from Talang Tuwo is niyur, meaning “coconut palm.” Cœdès prints it in his transcription of line 2 among the garden’s trees. These Latin letters are a scholarly transliteration of the 684 inscription’s South Indian-derived writing, not the original letterforms. A familiar plant connects the royal text with practical food-growing concerns.

ending.text: There was no common fall in 800. Sungai Mas continued as a port beyond the eighth century, and the regions followed different political and religious paths. Later atlas labels and named states must be read as new scopes, not the disappearance of these communities.
